stages.title: Ancient Greek philosophy
stages.hook: Thales said everything is made of water. Was that science, philosophy, or a guess? What would count as a good reason either way?
explain: Ancient Greek philosophy began, in the writings we have, around 600 BCE in cities along the coast of what is now Turkey and in Greek lands. Early thinkers called the Presocratics tried to explain the world through reasons instead of only stories about gods. Thales suggested that water is the basic stuff; Anaximander proposed the apeiron, the "unlimited"; Heraclitus stressed constant change and a rational order (logos); Parmenides argued that what is real cannot change; Democritus proposed that the world is made of atoms and empty space.

Some thinkers, the Sophists, taught argument and public speaking for pay. Protagoras is linked with the claim that "man is the measure of all things", which many read as a form of relativism. Socrates challenged them by asking whether there is a real knowledge of justice and goodness.

Plato and then Aristotle built large systems. Plato explored Forms, the soul and justice. Aristotle studied logic, nature, ethics and politics and founded the Lyceum. Greek philosophy matters because it started habits we still use: giving arguments, defining terms and testing ideas. It also influenced Islamic, Jewish and Christian thought, which carried and changed it.

example.q: Heraclitus says you cannot step into the same river twice. Parmenides says change is an illusion. What is their disagreement?
steps: Heraclitus: everything flows and changes.
Parmenides: what truly is does not change.
They disagree about whether change is real.
Later thinkers tried to solve this, for example with atoms or Forms.
example.a: They disagree about whether change is real or only appearance.

analogies.city: A busy harbour changes every hour, yet we call it the same harbour. That is the problem of change and sameness.
analogies.sea: Waves keep moving but the sea is still the sea. Heraclitus and Parmenides would describe this differently.
analogies.music: A song changes note by note but is still one song, a puzzle about unity and change.

stages.mnemonic: Presocratics ask What is the world made of? Sophists ask Can I persuade? Socrates asks What is the good?
terms: Early Greek thinkers before or around the time of Socrates who looked for natural explanations.
A Greek word meaning reason, account or word; Heraclitus used it for the rational order behind change.
The view, from Democritus, that things are made of tiny indivisible particles and void.
A teacher of rhetoric and argument in ancient Greece.
The view that some truths, such as moral truths, depend on a person or culture.

misc.wrong: The ancient Greeks invented philosophy and nobody else did.
misc.right: Greek philosophy is one early tradition among several. Thinkers in India, China and elsewhere were also reasoning about these questions.

stages.limits: The Presocratics survive mostly in fragments and later reports, so many interpretations of what they meant are debated.

questions.model: Heraclitus says change is real and everything flows. Parmenides argues that real being does not change, so change is only appearance. They disagree about the reality of change.
questions.why: This puzzle shaped later Greek thought.

questions.why: Atomists tried to reconcile permanence and change.

panel.why: Evidence is limited.

panel.q: Why are Sophists and Socrates often contrasted? Give one difference.
panel.model: Sophists often taught persuasive speaking for payment, while Socrates asked whether there is real knowledge of goodness and justice, though scholars note the picture is simplified.
panel.why: The contrast is traditional but contested.

panel.q: Why does the Greek tradition matter for later thinkers in Islamic and Christian worlds?
o: They studied, translated and answered Greek texts

panel.why: Texts were translated and developed in Arabic, Syriac and Latin.

teach.model: Early Greek thinkers looked for reasons about the world instead of just myths. Thales said water, Heraclitus change, Parmenides stillness, Democritus atoms. Socrates, Plato and Aristotle built on them. For example, the debate about whether change is real.

points.ask: What did they try to do?

stages.title: Hellenistic philosophy and Stoicism
stages.hook: If you lost your phone, your job and your money, what would still be in your control? Make a list.
explain: After Aristotle, in the Hellenistic period (roughly the 300s to 30 BCE), several schools taught how to live well in uncertain times. Epicureans, following Epicurus (341 to 270 BCE), said the good life is pleasure understood as peace of mind and freedom from pain. He valued friendship, simple living and not fearing death or gods; he did not mean endless luxury.

Stoicism was founded by Zeno of Citium around 300 BCE and was taught at the Stoa, a painted porch in Athens. Later Stoics include Seneca, Epictetus, and the emperor Marcus Aurelius. Stoics said virtue (wisdom, justice, courage, self-control) is the only true good, and that we should live in agreement with nature and reason. Epictetus taught that some things are up to us (our judgements and choices) and some are not (our health, wealth, other people).

Other schools included the Cynics, such as Diogenes, who lived simply and challenged social customs, and the Sceptics, who suspended judgement when arguments seemed equal. Scholars debate how far the Stoic view means we should not feel emotions. Stoics said we should not be ruled by harmful passions, but they still valued good feelings such as joy and goodwill.

example.q: A storm cancels your match. How would a Stoic respond?
steps: Separate what you control: your attitude and effort.
You do not control the weather.
So accept it and decide how to use the time.
example.a: Accept the weather; control your response.

analogies.sport: A runner cannot control the other runners, only training and effort. That is the Stoic focus.
analogies.sea: A sailor cannot control wind but can adjust sails.
analogies.home: You cannot control a friend's mood, but you can choose your own words.

stages.mnemonic: Stoic sorting: up to me, or not up to me?
terms: A school teaching that the good life is peace of mind and freedom from pain, with friendship and simplicity.
A school teaching that virtue is the only true good and we should live by reason.
A school of living simply and rejecting empty social conventions.
Suspending judgement when evidence is balanced.
Epictetus's division between what is up to us and what is not.

misc.wrong: Stoics want people to feel nothing.
misc.right: Stoics aimed to avoid being ruled by harmful passions, not to remove all feeling. They valued goodwill and joy in virtue.

stages.limits: Scholars debate how Stoic and Epicurean teachings were practised and how to translate key terms.

questions.model: If we focus on our own choices and accept what we cannot control, we spend less energy worrying about things we cannot change.
questions.why: It is a practical idea for steadiness.

questions.q: Is it accurate to call Epicurus a pure party-lover?

o: Acting justly is up to us and is a virtue

panel.q: Compare how an Epicurean and a Stoic might each handle losing a prized possession.
panel.model: Epicurean: realise we need little for happiness and focus on friendship and peace. Stoic: possessions are not up to us, so virtue and our judgement matter most. Both aim for calm.
panel.why: They share aims but give different reasons.

o: It claimed natural simplicity is better than status

teach.model: Stoics focus on what is up to us: our judgements and actions. Epicureans seek peace of mind. Cynics live simply. Sceptics hold back judgement. For example, accepting weather but controlling effort.

stages.title: Medieval European philosophy
stages.hook: Can faith and reason work together, or must you choose one? What would a thinker living in a time of great cathedrals say?
explain: Medieval European philosophy (roughly 400 to 1400 CE) was shaped by Christian thought but also by Greek texts. Augustine of Hippo (354 to 430), who lived in North Africa, wrote about time, evil, free will and the inner life in works such as the Confessions. Boethius (about 480 to 524) wrote the Consolation of Philosophy, about fortune and happiness, while in prison.

In the 1100s and 1200s, Aristotle's works became widely studied in Latin Europe, partly through translations from Arabic, and universities grew. Thomas Aquinas (1225 to 1274) tried to combine Aristotle with Christian faith. He argued that faith and reason can work together and wrote about natural law, the idea that reason can discover basic moral principles. Anselm proposed the ontological argument for God; many philosophers, both religious and not, have criticised it.

William of Ockham (about 1287 to 1347) argued for nominalism (only individual things exist, not universals) and for simplicity in explanation, often called Ockham's razor. Christine de Pizan (about 1364 to about 1430) defended women's abilities and dignity in her Book of the City of Ladies. Medieval philosophy was not only "religion"; it contains careful logic, language theory and ethics.

example.q: An argument claims "the simplest explanation is usually the best starting point". Which medieval thinker is linked with it?
steps: It is called Ockham's razor.
William of Ockham is associated with the principle.
The wording came later, but the idea fits his approach.

analogies.city: A cathedral rises over generations; medieval thinkers also built big systems of thought together.
analogies.nature: A scholar studies a leaf, then a star, and asks how reason and creation fit.
analogies.music: Plainchant has few notes but great structure, like an argument built with limited elements.

stages.mnemonic: Augustine looks in, Aquinas builds a bridge, Ockham trims the hedge.
terms: A medieval method of careful argument and debate in schools and universities.
The idea that reason can find basic moral principles from human nature.
The view that universals are names, and only individuals exist.
An argument that God exists from the idea of a greatest possible being.

misc.wrong: Medieval thinkers just repeated old authorities.
misc.right: Medieval thinkers debated sharply, introduced new logic and criticised each other and Aristotle.

stages.limits: The "Middle Ages" label is a European one, and philosophers elsewhere (such as Islamic and Jewish thinkers) were also active. Some of Aquinas' arguments remain contested.

trip.prompt: Find which thinkers wrote about faith and reason.

panel.model: Aquinas held that reason and faith can both lead toward truth, so careful reason need not conflict with faith, although each has its own domain.
panel.why: Many philosophers, religious or not, disagree on this.

panel.q: Why is the label "Middle Ages" limited?
o: It centres Europe and misses other regions

panel.why: Other regions had their own histories.

teach.model: Medieval thinkers like Augustine, Aquinas and Ockham used reason and faith together, studied Aristotle, and argued carefully. Ockham favoured simple explanations. For example, the razor says do not add needless causes.

stages.title: Islamic philosophical traditions
stages.hook: If a person had no senses at all, would they still know they exist? One philosopher imagined exactly this. What do you think he concluded?
explain: Islamic philosophy grew from the 8th century onwards, especially in cities such as Baghdad, Cairo, Córdoba and Samarkand. In Baghdad, scholars translated Greek works into Arabic. Al-Kindi (about 801 to 873) is often called the first major philosopher in the Arabic tradition. Al-Farabi (about 870 to 950) wrote on logic and on the ideal city.

Ibn Sina, known in Latin as Avicenna (980 to 1037), wrote on medicine and philosophy. His "flying man" thought experiment imagines a person created in mid-air with no sensation, and asks whether they would still be aware of themselves; he used it to argue that the self is not only the body. Al-Ghazali (1058 to 1111) wrote The Incoherence of the Philosophers, criticising some views of the philosophers. Ibn Rushd (Averroes, 1126 to 1198) answered him with The Incoherence of the Incoherence and wrote influential commentaries on Aristotle.

Ibn Khaldun (1332 to 1406) wrote the Muqaddimah, a study of history and society. He discussed how groups bond and how states rise and decline, using the idea of asabiyya (social solidarity). Islamic philosophy includes many schools, such as Suhrawardi's illuminationism and Mulla Sadra's views on existence. It also shaped Jewish and Latin European thought.

example.q: Ibn Sina imagines a person floating with no sensations. If they still know they exist, what might that suggest?
steps: They are aware of themselves without senses.
So self-awareness may not depend only on the body.
This is an argument, and critics offer objections.
example.a: It suggests the self may not be only the body (a debated argument).

analogies.city: Baghdad's scholars translated and debated books from many lands, like a great international library.
analogies.farm: Ibn Khaldun noted how settled and nomadic communities differ, as farms and herders often do.
analogies.tech: A philosophical thought experiment is like a simulation: it tests an idea in a controlled imagined case.

stages.mnemonic: Kindi starts, Farabi plans, Sina floats, Ghazali doubts, Rushd replies, Khaldun explains history.
terms: The period when Greek and other works were translated into Arabic.
An imagined case used to test an idea.
Ibn Khaldun's term for social solidarity that holds a group together.
The theme of Al-Ghazali's critique of some philosophers' arguments.

misc.wrong: Islamic philosophers only copied the Greeks.
misc.right: They criticised and developed Greek ideas and added original arguments in logic, metaphysics, medicine and social theory.

stages.limits: Interpreters disagree about the extent of Al-Ghazali's criticism of philosophy and about how to read Ibn Sina's flying man.

panel.model: He looked for patterns and causes in how groups, economies and states rise and decline, rather than only telling stories of rulers, which resembles later social science.
panel.why: Scholars discuss how to label his work.

panel.q: Why is it too simple to say Al-Ghazali "ended" philosophy in Islam?
o: Philosophy continued with Ibn Rushd, Suhrawardi, Mulla Sadra and others
Philosophy ended once he wrote his book

teach.model: Islamic philosophers translated and developed Greek ideas. Ibn Sina imagined a floating man to explore the self. Al-Ghazali criticised philosophers and Ibn Rushd replied. Ibn Khaldun studied history. For example, the flying man thought experiment.

What is a famous thought experiment?

stages.title: Jewish philosophical traditions
stages.hook: Can you treat a person as an "it" or only as a "you"? One Jewish philosopher thought this difference changes everything.
explain: Jewish philosophy has developed over many centuries in different lands, often in conversation with Greek, Islamic and European thought. Saadia Gaon (882 to 942), writing in Arabic in Babylonia, argued that reason and revelation can agree. Judah Halevi (about 1075 to 1141) wrote the Kuzari, defending Jewish tradition and stressing lived religious experience over pure reasoning.

Maimonides (1138 to 1204), born in Córdoba and later living in Egypt, wrote the Guide for the Perplexed. He argued that God cannot be described like a human and that talk about God needs careful interpretation. Baruch Spinoza (1632 to 1677), born in Amsterdam, argued that God and Nature are one substance; he was expelled from his Jewish community in 1656 and remains a major figure of modern philosophy.

In the 20th century, Franz Rosenzweig wrote The Star of Redemption, Martin Buber wrote I and Thou, describing two ways of relating: I-It (treating as an object) and I-Thou (meeting as a person). Emmanuel Levinas argued that ethics begins in the face-to-face encounter with another person, who makes a demand on us. These thinkers often connect ethics with responsibility to others.

example.q: A shopkeeper treats every customer only as a source of money. Which of Buber's ideas describes this?
steps: Treating as an object is I-It.
Meeting as a person is I-Thou.
So it is an I-It relationship.
example.a: I-It, though Buber says life includes both.

analogies.home: Talking with grandma, truly listening to her story, is I-Thou. Telling her to pass the salt is I-It, and both are normal.
analogies.city: A doctor who looks at a chart (I-It) and then sits and listens (I-Thou) uses both ways.
analogies.nature: Looking at a tree as timber is I-It; standing before it in awe may be I-Thou.

stages.mnemonic: Buber: It or Thou? Levinas: look at the face. Maimonides: do not make God a man.
terms: A claim that truth is made known by God.
Buber's term for a meeting between persons in which each is fully present.
Buber's term for relating to something as an object or tool.
Levinas's term for the person who makes an ethical claim on me.

misc.wrong: Jewish philosophy is only about religion.
misc.right: Jewish philosophers wrote on logic, ethics, politics, language and metaphysics, sometimes in dialogue with secular thought.

stages.limits: Interpreters disagree on how to read Maimonides' negative theology and on how Spinoza relates to Jewish thought.

panel.why: It stresses the limits of language about God.

panel.q: How could I-Thou thinking affect how we treat strangers?
panel.model: It invites us to meet strangers as whole persons, not as objects or tools, with respect and attention.

panel.why: He sees both as part of life.

teach.model: Jewish thinkers like Maimonides, Spinoza, Buber and Levinas wrote about God, nature, and ethics. Buber contrasted I-Thou and I-It. Levinas said ethics begins with facing another person. For example, listening to a patient as a person.

stages.title: Indian philosophical traditions
stages.hook: If you could look hard at your "self" and find nothing fixed there, would that be frightening or freeing? Different Indian traditions answered differently.
explain: Indian philosophy includes many schools that argue with each other. The Upanishads (composed over many centuries, from roughly 800 to 500 BCE for the earliest ones) explore Brahman, the ultimate reality, and Atman, the self. Several schools of Vedanta interpret their relation: Shankara (about 8th century CE) taught Advaita, non-dualism, saying Atman and Brahman are ultimately one; Ramanuja (11th to 12th century) taught that the self is a real part or mode of Brahman, a qualified non-dualism; Madhva taught dualism.

Buddhist philosophy began with the Buddha (about the 5th century BCE), who taught the Four Noble Truths about suffering and its end, and the idea of anatta (no fixed self). Nagarjuna later argued that things lack independent existence, called emptiness (shunyata). Jain philosophy, linked with Mahavira, stresses ahimsa (non-harm) and the many-sidedness of truth (anekantavada).

Nyaya developed logic and theories of knowledge with ways of knowing (pramanas), such as perception, inference, comparison and testimony. Charvaka, a materialist school, questioned inference and the afterlife. These schools debated openly; a good Indian philosopher had to know the opponent's views. Scholars note that "Indian philosophy" covers many traditions and that its dates and texts are discussed.

example.q: A blind-folded group touch an elephant; one says it is a rope (tail), one a wall (side). Which Jain idea fits?
steps: Each has part of the truth.
The truth has many sides.
This is anekantavada.

analogies.home: Siblings describe the same event differently; each sees a different side.
analogies.city: Bus riders see the same city from different windows.
analogies.nature: A river is one thing, but from the bank, a boat and the air it looks different.

stages.mnemonic: Atman is the self; Brahman is the whole; Buddha asks if the self is real; Jain says see many sides; Nyaya checks the proof.
terms: The self, in Upanishadic and Vedanta thought.
The Buddhist teaching that there is no fixed, unchanging self.
Non-harm, a key principle in Jain, Buddhist and Hindu ethics.
A means of knowing, such as perception or inference.

misc.wrong: All Indian philosophy says the same thing.
misc.right: Indian schools disagree strongly, for instance on whether the self exists, or whether the world is real.

stages.limits: Dates are uncertain for many early texts and teachers, and scholars debate how to translate terms like Brahman and shunyata.

questions.model: A Jain thinker would say each view captures part of reality from one standpoint, so we should listen to many perspectives, while not saying every view is correct.
questions.why: Scholars note that anekantavada is not simple relativism.

questions.q: Why might the elephant story help avoid arguments?
o: It reminds us we may each see only part
It says that no one can be right
It says that thinking should stop
It says that elephants are really ropes

panel.q: A critic says, "If there is no self, who is reborn or who suffers?" How is this question used?
o: It is a classic challenge Buddhist thinkers discuss
It has no answer and is ignored
It is a silly question that shows that the Buddhist view is simply wrong
It is a question only about elephants
panel.why: Buddhist schools discuss this carefully.

panel.q: Why is open debate between schools a feature of Indian philosophy?
panel.model: Philosophers had to understand and answer opponents' views, so schools developed careful logic and arguments in debate.
panel.why: This helped refine each school.

panel.q: Why is "Indian philosophy" a broad label?
o: It covers many schools, religions and secular views
It names one single book that all Indian thinkers wrote together
It is a name invented only in modern times
panel.why: It includes diverse traditions.

teach.model: Indian schools include Vedanta, Buddhism, Jainism, Nyaya and Charvaka. They argue about the self, reality and how we know. Jains stress non-harm and many sides of truth. For example, the elephant story.

stages.title: Chinese philosophical traditions
stages.hook: Should we love everyone equally, or care more for family first? Ancient Chinese thinkers argued about this.
explain: In ancient China during the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods (about 770 to 221 BCE) many schools of thought arose, often called the Hundred Schools. Confucius taught moral growth through ren and li. Mencius argued that human nature has a good beginning, like sprouts that need care. Xunzi argued that human nature needs training by learning and ritual.

Mozi (Mohism) argued for impartial care for all and criticised wasteful ritual and war; he judged actions by whether they benefit people. Daoism, in the Daodejing (attributed to Laozi) and the Zhuangzi, speaks of the Dao, the way, and of wu wei, acting in harmony without forcing. Zhuangzi is known for stories such as dreaming of being a butterfly. Legalism, with Han Feizi, argued that clear laws and rewards and punishments keep order.

These schools influenced each other. Later, Neo-Confucianism combined Confucian ethics with ideas about cosmos and mind. Scholars note that the traditions are debated and that categories like "Daoism" were drawn later. Chinese philosophy shows that ethics, politics and nature can be thought of together.

example.q: A village must decide how to share a limited harvest. How might each school respond?
steps: Confucian: care in graded relationships and moral leadership.
Mohist: care impartially, aiming at benefit for all.
Legalist: clear rules for everyone.
Daoist: avoid forcing and respond to circumstances.
example.a: Each gives a different practical emphasis.

analogies.farm: A farmer works with seasons rather than against them, a bit like wu wei.
analogies.city: A city with clear laws and fair officials echoes Legalist aims.
analogies.nature: A river finds its way around rocks, an image used in Daoist writings.

stages.mnemonic: Confucius cultivates, Mozi cares for all, Laozi flows, Han Feizi rules.
terms: The way; in Daoism, the natural pattern of things.
Acting without forcing, in harmony with circumstances.
The school stressing clear laws, rewards and punishments.

misc.right: Many schools, including Mohism, Daoism and Legalism, shaped Chinese thought and debated each other.

stages.limits: The authorship and dating of texts like the Daodejing are debated, and school labels were often applied later.

trip.prompt: Find the names of schools and pick one to describe.

questions.q: Who argued for impartial care for all?
Wu wei means...
questions.why: It is effortless action in harmony.

questions.q: Mencius thought human nature...
o: Has good sprouts that need care
Is hopeless and cannot be improved
Is only evil from the very start
Is empty and has no qualities

questions.q: Which school stressed laws, rewards and punishments?
questions.why: Han Feizi is linked with it.

questions.q: Xunzi argued that human nature...
o: Needs training through learning and ritual
Is already perfect at birth, so it needs no training or effort
Flows like a river without effort

questions.q: The Zhuangzi is known for stories like...
o: A lost sword found in a lake
A golden crown worn by a king
A flying carpet over the sea

questions.q: Match school and aim.
Why do Mohists criticise war and lavish ritual?
o: They judge actions by benefit to people
They like waste and show, and think ritual is the highest good

questions.q: Compare Confucian and Mohist views on how to care for people.
questions.model: Confucians emphasise care that starts with close relationships such as family and extends outward, while Mohists argue for impartial care for everyone equally.
questions.why: Both want a good society; they disagree on how.

questions.q: Why is "wu wei" often misunderstood as laziness?
o: It is about skilled action without strain, not inaction
It means sleeping through the day and letting others do the work
It is a rule to stop all action
It is a kind of tax
questions.why: It resembles a master craftsperson's ease.

panel.q: Does a Legalist think people are naturally good?
o: Han Feizi stressed self-interest and clear incentives
Yes, he thought that people were naturally good and needed no laws
He thought nobody had any nature
panel.why: He thought rules and incentives were needed.

panel.q: Why might Daoist and Confucian approaches complement each other?
panel.model: Confucian thought guides social duty and virtue, while Daoist thought values spontaneity and nature, so together they balance structure and flexibility.
panel.why: Many people in China drew on both.

panel.q: What is a fair statement about the label "Daoism"?
o: It was applied later to texts that differ in views
It was always the name of one single school
It is a modern invention with no texts
panel.why: Scholars discuss the categories.

teach.model: Chinese schools include Confucianism, Mohism, Daoism and Legalism. Confucius stressed moral growth, Mozi impartial care, Daoists harmony with the Dao, and Legalists clear laws. For example, sharing a harvest.

stages.title: African philosophical traditions
stages.hook: Is wisdom only in books? Some African philosophers collected and studied the wisdom of village elders. Why?
explain: Africa has many philosophical traditions, written and oral. Ancient Egyptian wisdom texts taught Maat: truth, justice and balance. In Ethiopia, Zera Yacob (1599 to 1692) is known from a text, the Hatata, in which he reasons by his own mind about God and ethics and argues for equal dignity of people; some scholars have questioned its authorship and date, while many defend it. Anton Wilhelm Amo, born in what is now Ghana, studied in Germany in the 1700s and wrote on mind and body.

Oral traditions hold philosophical ideas in proverbs, myths and sayings. Akan thought (Ghana) has concepts of the person, and Kwasi Wiredu argued for "conceptual decolonization", examining African concepts in their own languages. Yoruba thought has ideas about destiny and character (iwa). Sophie Oluwole studied Yoruba thought and Ifá. Henry Odera Oruka recorded "sage philosophy" with thoughtful elders in Kenya. Paulin Hountondji criticised treating African thought as one shared folk belief.

Political thinkers such as Julius Nyerere (ujamaa, familyhood), Kwame Nkrumah and Léopold Senghor (negritude) linked philosophy to freedom and development. Frantz Fanon wrote about colonialism and psychology. Scholars debate whether to speak of "African philosophy" as a whole, because of Africa's many peoples and different views.

example.q: Elders in a village discuss what a good leader is. How might this be philosophy?
steps: They give reasons and examples.
They compare ideas and test them with experience.
Oruka called such thinking sage philosophy.
example.a: Careful reasoning, even when oral, is philosophy.

analogies.home: Proverbs at home carry advice and reasons, like short arguments.
analogies.farm: Communal farming teaches cooperation and fairness.
analogies.city: A council of elders listens to both sides of a dispute.

stages.mnemonic: Maat balances; Zera Yacob reasons; Wiredu clarifies concepts; Oruka listens to sages.
terms: Ancient Egyptian idea of truth, justice and cosmic order.
Oruka's term for reflective thinking by wise individuals in oral cultures.
Nyerere's Swahili term for familyhood, a vision of cooperative community.
Wiredu's call to examine concepts in African languages and thought.

misc.right: Philosophy can be oral. Reasoned argument can be spoken, recorded or written.

stages.limits: Debates continue about the authorship of the Hatata and about whether African thought forms one tradition or many.

trip.prompt: Find three named philosophers and their countries.

questions.q: What is Maat?
o: Truth, justice and balance in ancient Egypt
A language of ancient Egypt used only by priests and kings
questions.why: It was a moral and cosmic principle.

questions.q: Who is associated with "sage philosophy"?
Zera Yacob is known as a thinker from...
questions.why: He is linked with the Hatata.

questions.q: What does ujamaa mean?
questions.why: Nyerere used it for cooperative community.

questions.q: Anton Wilhelm Amo was born in what is now...
questions.why: He studied in Germany in the 1700s.

questions.q: Wiredu is known for...
questions.why: He studied how African concepts work.

questions.q: Match person and region or idea.
Why do some scholars question the Hatata's authorship?
o: Its origin and date are debated
It has no text at all
It is written in modern slang

questions.q: Why can oral proverbs count as philosophy?
questions.model: Proverbs and sayings can carry reasoned ideas about ethics, truth and community that are examined and debated, even without writing.
questions.why: The form does not decide whether it is philosophy.

questions.q: Why do scholars hesitate to say "African philosophy" is one thing?
o: Africa has many peoples with different traditions
Africa is a very small place with only one people and one view

panel.q: Hountondji worried about "ethnophilosophy". What was the concern?
o: Treating a whole people as sharing one unquestioned system of belief
That Africans have no ideas and so need ideas to be brought in
panel.why: He stressed individual critical argument.

panel.q: Explain how Oruka's sage philosophy answers the claim that Africa had no philosophy.
panel.model: Oruka showed that individual sages reasoned critically about ideas in oral cultures, which counts as philosophy even if not written.
panel.why: Some scholars debate whether all sages did philosophy.

panel.q: How do Nyerere and Fanon show philosophy linked to politics?
o: They wrote on freedom, community and colonialism
They were both famous chess players and ignored public affairs
They wrote cookbooks for the army
panel.why: Their ideas connect to action.

teach.model: African philosophy includes ancient Egyptian Maat, Zera Yacob, Amo, Akan and Yoruba thought, sage philosophy and political thinkers. Ideas can be oral or written. For example, elders reasoning about leadership.

stages.title: Indigenous philosophical and ethical traditions
stages.hook: If a river could be treated as a living ancestor, how would that change what people may do to it?
explain: Indigenous peoples across the world have many distinct philosophies, so any short summary has limits. Many traditions share themes of relationship, reciprocity and responsibility to land, water, animals, ancestors and future generations. Knowledge is often passed through story, song, ceremony and practice and is tied to place.

Examples: In Māori thought (Aotearoa New Zealand), whanaungatanga is kinship and connection, mana is authority and dignity, and kaitiakitanga is guardianship of the environment. In Andean traditions, ayni is reciprocity, and Pachamama is often translated as Mother Earth; the concept of sumak kawsay or buen vivir speaks of living well with community and nature. Many Aboriginal Australian peoples hold deep responsibilities to Country, meaning land with its stories and kin. Many Indigenous North American nations emphasise relations with human and other-than-human beings and responsibility for seven generations in some nations' teachings.

These ideas can challenge views that treat nature as only resources. They also inform law: a river in Aotearoa New Zealand, the Whanganui, was recognised in law as a legal person in 2017. Scholars warn against romanticising or stereotyping. Each nation has its own languages, laws and philosophies, and members themselves debate how to apply them today.

example.q: A community must decide whether to build a dam on a river central to their stories. How would an ethic of guardianship shape the question?
steps: Consider the river as kin and as a source of life.
Ask who is responsible to future generations.
Listen to those with knowledge of the place.
example.a: Guardianship leads to long-term, relationship-based questions.

analogies.nature: A forest teaches patience and cycles; many Indigenous traditions treat it as a relative, not just wood.
analogies.farm: A farmer who rotates crops to keep soil healthy shows a kind of reciprocity with land.
analogies.sea: Fishers who take only what they need and avoid emptying a fishing ground show respect for the sea.

stages.mnemonic: Relationship, reciprocity, responsibility: the three R of many Indigenous ethics.
terms: A Māori term for guardianship of the environment.
An Andean idea of reciprocal help.
In many Aboriginal Australian traditions, land with its stories, law and kin.
A Kichwa phrase often translated as living well in harmony with community and nature.

misc.wrong: All Indigenous peoples think the same thing.
misc.right: There are thousands of distinct nations with different philosophies, laws and languages.

stages.limits: These summaries are broad and cannot capture the specific teachings of each nation. Indigenous scholars and communities should be the main authorities on their own thought.

trip.prompt: Find examples of how Indigenous ideas appear in law or policy.

questions.q: What is kaitiakitanga?
o: A traditional dance of the sea
A fishing tool used in boats
A song sung before a war
questions.why: It is a Māori idea of guardianship.

questions.q: Ayni refers to...
o: A tax paid to a ruler
A mountain in the Andes that the community treats as sacred

questions.q: In 2017 the Whanganui River in Aotearoa New Zealand was...
o: Recognised in law as a legal person
Drained and turned into farmland for a nearby town
questions.why: This reflects Māori relationships with the river.

questions.q: "Country" in many Aboriginal Australian traditions means...
o: Land with stories, law and kin
A farm owned by a family

questions.q: Which theme is common across many Indigenous traditions?
o: Relationship and responsibility to land and others
Competition for wealth and individual advantage above all else
Fear of the sky and stars
A rule never to speak with elders

questions.q: Sumak kawsay is often translated as...
Match each term to its tradition.
Why do scholars warn against saying "Indigenous people believe X"?
o: Nobody in any Indigenous community believes anything at all
They have no beliefs at all

questions.q: How might an ethic of reciprocity change the way people use a forest?
questions.model: People would think about giving back and taking only what is needed, caring for the forest for future generations rather than treating it as endless resources.
questions.why: This is a general illustration, not any one nation's law.

questions.q: Why is knowledge often tied to place in these traditions?
o: Stories and responsibilities belong to particular lands
Maps of places are kept secret from everyone outside the community

panel.q: A critic says legal personhood for a river is strange. What can be said?
o: It expresses a relationship in law and gives a way to protect the river
It makes rivers speak in court as witnesses on their own behalf
It is only a joke with no meaning
It has no effect on anyone
panel.why: The law appoints guardians to act for the river.

panel.q: Why should we hear Indigenous people speak for their own traditions?
panel.model: They hold the knowledge and can describe it accurately; outsiders may stereotype or misrepresent, so respect and accuracy call for their voices.
panel.why: This is also an ethical point about respect.

panel.q: Which statement about Indigenous philosophies is fair?
o: They are diverse and living traditions
They are only ancient and have ended
They are all one single belief
They are finished and no longer practised
panel.why: Traditions continue and change.

teach.model: Many Indigenous nations stress relationship, reciprocity and responsibility to land and people. Examples include kaitiakitanga, ayni and Country. Each nation is different. For example, the Whanganui River legal status.
